title.en: The Bungling Host: Coyote Visits his Sons-in-Law
title.zh: 笨拙之主：郊狼拜訪女婿

region.en: Winter ice-holes of the Sahaptin rivers (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩哈普廷諸河冬季冰洞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 10. The Bungling Host'

summary.en: Visiting Deer, Elk and Fish-Hawk with his son, Coyote sees each son-in-law's magic — Deer cuts his wife's dress to boil into fat meat, Elk extracts a gut from his own body that cooks into canvas-back duck, Fish-Hawk dives through an ice-hole with five switches and comes up strung with fish — and tries to repeat each trick at home: his wife's dress stays buckskin, his excrements stay excrement, and he jumps at the ice and nearly kills himself. The sons-in-law cook for the family each time and go home in disgust, while Coyote lies unconscious on the ice and recovers only to have the fish cooked 'for he had nearly lost his life getting them.'
summary.zh: 郊狼偕子拜訪鹿、麋、魚鷹三位女婿。鹿割妻裙入沸水即化肥肉；麋自體取腸，煮成帆背鴨；魚鷹持五枝潛入冰洞，出而滿掛游魚。郊狼逐一效仿：割妻裙，裙仍為皮；取糞，糞仍是糞；躍冰取魚，幾乎喪命。眾女婿每至皆為其家治膳，食畢憤然離去；郊狼昏臥冰上，醒後猶令其妻烹魚——『吾幾為此喪命。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. A second version with Kingfisher, Elk, Beaver, Wolf and Mountain-Sheep is recorded in the source. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote lived with his family, and had several daughters: one had married the Deer, one the Elk, and one the Fish-Hawk. One day Coyote said to his son, 'Let us visit your sister, Deer's wife!' When they arrived there, Deer said to his wife, 'Build a fire and heat stones.' She did as bidden and boiled the water; then Deer took his knife and cut a piece from her dress, cut it to pieces, and threw it into the water — as soon as he had cut it, it grew right down again. Coyote said to himself, 'I am not going to eat an old dirty dress like that!' Soon it boiled and turned into fat deer-meat, and Deer's wife took it out and set it before her father. Coyote invited his daughter and her husband Deer to come and see him the next day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 164 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next day Coyote's daughter and her husband came. Coyote said to his wife, 'Build a fire and heat stones.' When the water boiled, Coyote cut pieces from his wife's dress and threw them into the water; the pieces, however, remained buckskin, nor did the dress grow out again. So Deer said to his wife, 'Let us do it for them and go home!' They did so and went home. Next day Coyote said to his son, 'Let us go and visit your sister, Elk's wife!' Elk said to his wife, 'Cut me a green stick'; he bent it over, tied it together, and covered it with ashes; then he asked for a basket, took a stick, and extracted dung from his own body. Coyote asked, 'Am I to eat that stick and my son-in-law's excrements?' They continued cooking the dung, which turned into canvas-back duck; when they took the stick out, it proved to be an intestine filled with meat, so they ate it. 'Come and visit us to-morrow!' said Coyote.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 164-165 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: When they arrived on the following day, Coyote cut a green stick, bent it with difficulty, and extracted two mice which he had hidden. Then he struck the wood: the wood burned and sprang apart, scattering sparks over Coyote's wife and setting fire to her. She ran out; Elk and his wife prepared the food and went home in disgust, and Coyote ate the food himself. Next morning Coyote asked his son to go with him to see his brother-in-law, Fish-Hawk, whose wife built a fire, and Fish-Hawk perched on a tree that grew up through a hole in the ice, called, dived, and came up again with several strings of fish, which his wife cooked for her guests.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 165 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The following day they came, and Coyote, who had an old tree in the ice, cut a hole as his son-in-law had done, told his wife to get sticks, climbed the tree, and jumped — 'Oh, see my father jump! He has missed the hole and has killed himself!' cried the boy. Fish-Hawk's wife said, 'Go and get fish for them'; Fish-Hawk did so, and then he and his wife left them. Coyote lay unconscious on the ice; soon he recovered, and told his wife to cook the fish for him, for he had nearly lost his life getting them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 165 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote and Fox: The Pitch Log, the Wounded Deer, and the Frozen Tail
title.zh: 郊狼與狐：松脂之木、傷鹿與凍尾

region.en: Winter camps of the Sahaptin (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩哈普廷冬季營地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 11. Coyote and Fox'

summary.en: Fox shares sparingly, then admits his secrets one by one: split pitch-wood backward and it becomes dried salmon; trail tricks bring rabbits; drag the tail through a running ice-riffle and it comes out strung with roots. Coyote works each trick to his own ruin — splitting pitch all day for nothing until Fox's own cache spoils too; imitating the wounded-deer trick by breaking the hunter's arrow, so the deer jumps up, kicks him over, and he comes home covered with blood; and, imitating the root-trick, has his tail freeze into the riffle and drag him down the stream, where he drowns until Fox finds him lodged in the ice, drags him out, and walks back and forth over him several times, which brings him to life.
summary.zh: 狐吝而後漸吐其秘：松脂木向後劈之即成鮭乾；詭計可誘兔；尾探冰流，拔出則掛根一串。郊狼逐一效尤，反自取其辱：劈脂終日而無所獲，且連累狐之窖藏亦化松脂；仿傷鹿計而折其箭，鹿躍起踢翻郊狼，血污而歸；仿取根計，尾凍冰中，被拖入激流，溺斃——狐尋至冰中，拖出其屍，往返踐踏數遍，郊狼方蘇。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. One crude rabbit-catching episode in the source is omitted from this record. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote and Fox lived together. Coyote used to hunt mice and gather wild-rose berries, and would share them with Fox, giving him only a few, however, saying that he had not been able to get many. Every evening he would see Fox eating, and once he jumped at him and asked what he was eating — 'Oh, salmon,' was the reply. Fox refused to tell where he got them, but finally explained that he had found a log with pitch on it, that he had split off a few pieces, thrown them backward, and that these had become dried salmon. Coyote said that he was strong, and that he was going to work the next day in order to procure a winter supply.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 168 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Early the next morning Coyote went to Fox's log, found a small piece of dried salmon, ate it, split two other logs, and ate the salmon that came from these. After that, he worked all day without ever looking back; when evening came and he looked about, nothing but pitch-wood was to be seen. He was thoroughly disgusted, but carried a load home. Fox had stayed at home; when he went to his cache, he too found that everything there was pitch-wood: 'There,' he said, 'Coyote has spoiled everything!' When Coyote arrived with his load of pitch-wood, Fox told him that he had not gone about it in the right manner — when he, Fox, had split enough, he had always turned around and seen the salmon, and then returned home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 168-169 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day Fox went out and met a wounded deer that dropped down right in front of him; Fox took an arrow out of the deer's side, and when the hunter came up the trail and found him sitting down, he gave Fox the meat in gratitude. Coyote heard how it was done: 'Well, if he was afraid of you, he would be scared to death of me. I should frighten him by my looks.' So the next morning Coyote went, and the same thing happened, except that Coyote broke the arrow and threw it away; the man became angry, and gave the deer a kick. The deer jumped up and ran away, and as it did so, it kicked Coyote over; when he came home covered with blood, Fox asked him what was the matter, and told him what he ought to have done.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 169-170 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next morning Fox went down the trail to the river, dropped his tail into the creek, and when he drew it forth there were many roots attached to it. Old-Coyote watched Fox and pestered him until he told: 'I went down and got into the riffle. I stuck my tail in where the ice was running; and when I pulled it out, I drew these roots out with it.' — 'I can do that all day,' said Coyote. So the next morning Coyote went and found the place; he stuck his tail in and drew out a few roots, which he promptly ate. Then his tail froze in and dragged him down the stream; he could not disengage himself, and was drowned. Fox waited for him all day, then decided to look for him, found him lodged in the ice, dragged him out, and walked back and forth over him several times; this brought him to life, and they went home together.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 170 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Sweat-House Man and the Scare-Monster Scheme

region.en: Sweat-house by the river trail (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 河畔小道旁汗屋（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 11. Coyote and Fox' (the sweat-house man)

summary.en: Fox finds a sweat-house where a man steams himself and tells him to go to the camp, cook what he needs, and take home all he can carry; Coyote, boasting he is a great shaman, waits to be served — then kills the man, and at the same moment everything runs out of the tent, even the clothes and moccasins he was wearing, not a bit of meat left, and Coyote goes home naked and barefoot to Fox's 'You old fool! I did as the man told me — I cooked, and then I went home.' Later the pair kill an old woman, stuff her, and Coyote wears her on his head while Fox runs ahead crying the warning of a terrible monster whose voice means death — the people flee, the plunderrers feast, and in the second village the murdered woman's grand-daughter, knowing the trick, waits, takes her grandmother away from Coyote, and ends the game.
summary.zh: 狐遇河畔汗屋，屋主許其到營自炊自取。郊狼自詡大神，坐等奉侍——竟殺屋主；頃刻間帳中所有之物俱逃，連其身上衣履皆去，片肉無存。郊狼赤足裸身而歸，狐曰：『蠢材！我聽其言，炊而後歸。』後二人殺一老嫗，填之成偶，郊狼頂之於首，狐奔走告警：『恐怖怪獸將至，聞其聲者必死！』族人倉皇逃散，二人劫掠自肥。至第二村，老嫗之孫女知其詐，坐待其來，自郊狼頭上取回祖母，其計遂敗。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The next morning they both went different ways. Fox went down the river and found a sweat-house in which a man was taking a steam-bath; there was some grease in the sweat-house. The man told Fox to go to the camp and cook what he needed, and after eating to take home all he could carry. Fox did so and returned home. When Coyote arrived, he offered Fox two or three mice; Fox paid no attention to his gift, so Coyote ate them for spite. Later Coyote caught Fox eating meat, and after some persuasion Fox told Coyote what had happened. Then Coyote said, 'Well, I am a great shaman, and the man will know it and give me all the meat I can carry.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 170 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Early the next morning Coyote started. He came to the man in the sweat-house, who told him the same as he had told Fox on the previous day. Coyote went to the tent, and said to himself, 'Here is meat enough for you!' He cooked nothing, but waited for the man to come and cook for him, 'for he knows I am a shaman, and I shall not cook for myself.' The man came back, and, after getting breakfast for himself, went to sleep. Then Coyote grew angry, and said to himself, 'I will kill him!' So he killed the man; and at the same moment everything ran out of the tent, even the clothes and moccasins that he was wearing. Not a bit of meat nor anything else was left. Coyote wondered what it all meant; he went home naked and barefoot. Fox said to him, when he came, 'You old fool! I did not act that way. I did as the man told me — I cooked, and then I went home.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 170-171 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: After several days, Coyote said, 'Here we are getting hungry. Now, I have a plan. There is a village with many people. We can scare them away and live on the plunder for a year. There is an old woman on this side that we can kill. Then we can stuff her, and I can wear her on my head and so frighten the people. You can go ahead on a message.' They killed the woman and thought that she looked dreadful enough to frighten the people. When they were near the village, Coyote said to Fox, 'Now, go ahead with your message! Cry out, There is a terrible monster coming! Should any one hear its voice, that person will surely sicken and die. The only way to save yourselves is to run away. I am the only one that is safe, because I can outrun him. There he is now! Look at him!' Fox carried out his instructions to the letter; the people were frightened and ran away, Fox ran on ahead and hid himself, and later came back to find that Coyote had already taken all the best plunder.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 170-171 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The grand-daughter of the old woman whom they had killed lived in the second village they were going to visit. They started for it, as before; Fox again gave the warning, but the young woman did not run, for she knew what Coyote and Fox had done. She waited until they came; then she got up and took her grandmother away from Coyote. That is the end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 171 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Race for Life Against the Magpie Boys

region.en: Village race-course by the creek (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 村中溪畔賽道（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 11. Coyote and Fox' (the race for life)

summary.en: 'Let us go to the village and run a race with the people! ... we will race for life. If we win, we will cut their throats; and if they beat us, they may cut ours. You are safe in any case, for no animal can outrun you.' Four days of victories follow — the Deer boys, the Mountain-Sheep, the Elk boys, the white-tailed Deer — Coyote taking the lion's share each time; but on the fifth day, against Fox's warning, they race the Magpie boys and are beaten. Coyote hides near the creek, where playing boys cry, 'Oh, see Coyote hiding in the bushes!'; the Magpies, who had already killed Fox, find him with his nose sticking out of the water, drag him out and cut his throat.
summary.zh: 郊狼提議：『去村中賽跑，以命相搏；勝者斬敗者之頭。』連勝四日——鹿族少年、大角羊、麋族、白尾鹿——郊狼每次皆取大份。第五日，狐諫勿與喜鵲兄弟比賽，郊狼不聽，竟敗。郊狼匿於溪畔，戲童高呼：『看！郊狼藏在草叢裡！』喜鵲已誅狐，又尋得郊狼——其鼻猶露水面——拖出而斬其喉。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Once when Coyote lived with Fox, he said to him, 'Let us go to the village and run a race with the people! You are a good runner, and we shall win. I shall do the talking, and we will race for life. If we win, we will cut their throats; and if they beat us, they may cut ours. You are safe in any case, for no animal can outrun you.' — 'All right!' said Fox. They arrived at the village, and announced that they had come to race the Deer boys, and that the winners should cut off the heads of the losers. The five Deer boys raced Coyote and Fox, and the latter won; they killed the five deer, Coyote taking the three older ones, and Fox the two younger ones. The next day they went to the Mountain-Sheep, and the same happened; the third day they raced the Elk boys and beat them in the same manner; the fourth day they tried the white-tailed Deer and beat them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 171 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The fifth day Coyote said, 'Let us run against the Magpie boys!' — 'No,' said Fox, 'they will beat us. Of course, you can beat them,' Coyote assured him. 'No I cannot,' Fox insisted. 'Besides, they are of no use to us, even if we do win.' — 'Why, we want their feathers,' said Coyote. Nevertheless they did race with the Magpies, and were beaten. Coyote hid himself near the creek; some little boys who were playing there cried, 'Oh, see Coyote hiding in the bushes!' The Magpies had already killed Fox; they found Coyote, whose nose was sticking out of the water, dragged him out, and cut his throat. Coyote became a spirit. Whenever any woman came out to urinate or a couple to cohabit, he would call them by name. They grew tired of this, and finally resuscitated him. After this Coyote went off by himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 171 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 172 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

region.en: Polecat's lodge on the game trails (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 獸徑旁臭貓之居（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 11. Coyote and Fox' (Polecat and the game-people)

summary.en: Revived, Coyote comes to Polecat and his sister and teaches the trick: Polecat plays sick, the sister follows the trail of the Deer brothers crying that her brother is nearly dead and wants to see his friends, and when the five Deer go in, Polecat turns loose and kills them; Coyote butchers the meat, and the same is done to the White-Tailed Deer and the Mountain-Sheep. But when they try it on the Elk, the youngest Elk warns his brothers, takes the lead with his single antler, and as Polecat raises his tail, runs him through; Elk beats Polecat against a stump and leaves him, and his sister and Coyote come and find him dead.
summary.zh: 郊狼復活後遇臭貓兄妹，授計：臭貓裝病，其妹循鹿徑哭告『吾兄垂危，欲見故人』；五鹿入內探病，臭貓暴起誅之。郊狼剖肉而食。白尾鹿、大角羊亦如法炮製。及至麋族，幼麋先告諸兄：『吾有一角，本欲脫之，正好以此誅敵。』遂自領先入帳；臭貓舉尾之際，幼麋以角刺之。麋以臭貓屍擊樹樁而去。其妹與郊狼至，見其已死。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote came to the place where Polecat and his sister were living. He suggested to Polecat that he play sick: 'Then your sister must go and call in the Deer brothers to see you. When they come in, you can kill them with your stick.' — 'All right!' said Polecat. Coyote then told Polecat's sister to follow the Deer's trail, and when she came near them to call out, 'My brother is nearly dead and wants to see his friends!' She started out; and as the Deer came by, she cried, and said what Coyote had instructed her to say. The Deer said, 'We will come soon.' The sister then ran home and announced that the Deer were coming. Polecat played sick, and Coyote stepped out and said to the Deer, 'Go in and see your friend! This is the last time you will see him.' The five Deer went in, and Polecat turned loose and killed them; Coyote cut up the meat, and after that was gone, they did the same to the White-Tailed Deer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 172 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: After that Coyote said, 'Let us kill the Mountain-Sheep!' The sister played the same part as before; everything happened as on the previous occasions. Coyote was outside, and addressed them in the same manner, and Polecat killed them as he had the others. Next Coyote proposed trying the Elk. He told the sister to go and wait on their trail. She did everything just as she had done previously. The youngest Elk said he had something with which to kill them; he told his brothers all that had happened, and that the only way to get rid of Polecat was for him to take the lead: 'I have only one antler, and must take it off, anyway. I will kill him with that.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 172-173 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: They came to Polecat's tent, and Polecat got ready. Coyote spoke as before. The Elks, though, had everything arranged: the youngest one passed the others, and as Polecat raised his tail, he ran him through with his antler. Then Elk ran out of the tent. When the sister and Coyote saw the Polecat sticking on Elk's antler, they could not help laughing; finally Elk beat Polecat against a stump, and left him. His sister and Coyote came, and found him dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 173 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

region.en: Moon's house beyond the ring of the moon (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 月環之外的月神之居（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 12. Coyote kills the Moon'

summary.en: The Moon's son hunts people as men hunt deer and brings the bodies home for his father, who eats the testicles of every man the boy kills. Coyote befriends the boy, conjures a fine spring — 'Your father is my brother' — asks to hold his club while he drinks, and kills him with his own club; stripped and dressed in his clothes, he carries the body in a rawhide sack to Moon's house, where the old man eats his own son's testicles — 'They do not taste very good; they are too strong.' Coyote plans to leave with the fine ornaments, but cannot pass the ring around the moon — travelling all night brings him no farther than the door. On the third attempt the old man decides this is not his son: 'You have killed my son and brought me his body to eat.' Coyote answers: 'Henceforth you shall be a good moon and not kill people. They will know you, and you shall be good to them. The moon shall be up above and give light. People shall pass by unmolested hereafter' — and having first put the moon in the sky, he travels away.
summary.zh: 月神之子獵人如人獵鹿，攜屍歸家；其父食所誅男子之睪丸。郊狼佯與之交好，幻出甘泉——『令尊乃吾兄』——借其木棒觀賞，趁其俯身飲水，以棒擊斃之。剝衣扮之，負屍於皮囊至月神之居。老神食其子之睪丸，曰：『味不甚佳，太烈。』郊狼欲携珍寶而逃，然竟不能越月環——夜行整宿，猶在門邊。第三夜事敗，老神識破：『爾殺吾子，以其屍進吾食！』郊狼答曰：『自此爾當為良月，不得殺人。人將識爾，爾亦當善待之。月懸高天，普照大地，行人從此無虞。』郊狼先置月於天，然後遠行。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Moon-slaying episode; a second version (with the hot sun and five knives) is recorded in the source. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The Moon and his son lived together. The boy used to hunt people just as we are hunting for deer; he took the bodies home to the old man, who ate the testicles of all the men the boy killed. Coyote heard of this, and decided to kill him. One day, when the boy was out hunting, Coyote stole up from behind, and said, 'This is not the place you are looking for. Follow me, and I will show you where I used to hunt. Your father is my brother.' The Moon boy did not know what to say. Coyote said to him, 'We used to build a fire near here. I will show you the place. There is a fine spring near by' — and, lo! there was a spring. He guided the Moon there, and showed him the spring, which was exceedingly cold.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 173 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'I am very thirsty. Where is your tent?' Moon's son pointed it out. 'What do you take to the old man when you go home?' he asked. Moon's son replied, 'I give him testicles; he eats them.' Moon's son carried the club with which he used to kill people. Coyote said to him, 'Drink while I look at your club!' Then, as the youth stooped over, Coyote killed him with his own club. Coyote stripped him and put on his clothes — 'I look just like him,' he said — and carried a rawhide sack, into which he put the body of the youth. It began to grow dark just as he reached Moon's house. He entered, and saw a great fat old man; the house was filled with fine ornaments. The old man untied the pack and ate his own son's testicles. 'They do not taste very good,' he said; 'they are too strong.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 173 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote decided to leave the house that night and take with him the ornaments he saw; he ate some of the flesh of the Moon's son, but soon threw it aside. Then he lay down and waited for the old man to go to sleep, and soon he slept soundly. Coyote then took the ornaments and prepared to leave; he went as far as the door. It was evening, and he would have to travel all night; he was very tired, however, so he decided to rest a while and go on later, placing the ornaments at the head of his bed. The old man awoke, and saw Coyote lying near the door: Coyote had not even passed through the ring around the moon. He told the old man that he had walked in his sleep and that he was feeling very sick; the third day he tried again, but still he could not get farther than the door.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 173-174 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Finally the old man decided that this was not his son. He said to Coyote, 'You have killed my son and brought me his body to eat. I thought so at the time. Why did you kill him?' Coyote said to him, 'Henceforth you shall be a good moon and not kill people. They will know you, and you shall be good to them. The moon shall be up above and give light. People shall pass by unmolested hereafter.' The Moon agreed, and told him to go; he gave him clothes and presents and sent him away, telling him, 'It is daytime now, and you can travel far.' Then Coyote travelled, having first put the moon in the sky. Thus Coyote killed the Moon boy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 174 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Five Grizzly-Bear Girls and the Black-Bear Boy
title.zh: 五灰熊姊妹與黑熊之子

region.en: Root-digging canyons of the bear country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 熊鄉掘根之谷（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 13. The Bears'

summary.en: Five Grizzly-Bear girls, enraged that the oldest man married Black-Bear's daughter instead of them, dance with blood spurting from their mouths and vow to kill the men in spring; one by one the men are lured by a beautiful root-digging woman who becomes a wild grizzly and breaks their necks, four heads taken to the den. Black-Bear's son, accused by his father of wrong words in his dance-song, goes alone — 'for if they kill me, they will kill you as well' — shoots the first grizzly woman as she invites him near, then a second arrow as she makes for him; morning after morning he kills the sisters in the same way, all five. Then the old Black-Bear put the four heads back on their bodies, stepped over them, and thus restored them to life.
summary.zh: 五灰熊姊妹因長兄娶黑熊之女而憤，歌舞時口中噴血，誓於春季誅殺男人。諸男相繼為掘根美婦所誘——婦忽化為狂怒灰熊，扭斷其頸，四顆人頭被攜回熊穴。黑熊之子遭父斥責舞歌唱錯咒語，請命獨往——『若吾死，爾亦難逃』——待灰熊婦招其近前即放箭，再補一箭斃之。此後每晨誅一姊妹，五姐妹盡除。老黑熊將四顆人頭歸位，跨越其身，諸男遂復活。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Once upon a time there were five men and five Grizzly-Bear girls; there was also a Black-Bear who had a son and a daughter. The oldest man had married the daughter of Black-Bear. This angered the Grizzly-Bears, as they wanted the men for themselves. They became so enraged that they resolved to kill the men: they danced, and as they did so, blood spurted forth from their mouths, and they said, 'When spring comes, we shall kill them.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 175 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day, when the oldest man went hunting, he saw a woman digging roots in a canyon; when she held up her head, he saw that she was good-looking, with a high crown on her hat, beautifully dressed and painted, her hair long. He walked up the canyon toward her, wondering who she might be; she was really the oldest Grizzly-Bear girl. She asked the man to come near, and as he approached her, she became a wild grizzly bear, seized him and broke his neck. On the following day, when his brothers went to look for him, they found his body with broken neck. In the same way the Grizzly-Bears killed four of the men and took their heads to their den.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 175 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Black-Bear's son knew all that happened. His father accused him of having killed his brothers-in-law: 'You say the wrong things when you sing while you are dancing.' They danced, and the boy sang, saying that he would kill the first bear that came out — he sang the wrong words. The old Bear said, 'Go and look for your brother-in-law'; the girl then told him that four had been killed, and only one was left. 'Let us go and see them,' the man said. 'No, don't come! Let me go alone,' the boy replied, 'for if they kill me, they will kill you as well.' He went alone, and found the Grizzly-Bear woman digging roots; as he approached her, she invited him too to come up and talk.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 175-176 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The boy had been warned to shoot when she spoke to him; he did so and shot her. When she made for him, he shot a second arrow and killed her. Then he returned home. On the following morning he went again; this time another Grizzly-Bear was there digging roots. He approached her and killed her as he had killed her sister. The next morning he went again, and the same thing happened; thus he disposed of all five sisters. Then the old Black-Bear put the four heads of the men back on their bodies; he stepped over them, and thus restored them to life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 175-176 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Owl and the Widow's Children

region.en: Night trail to the canoe-maker's bank (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 赴造舟者河岸之夜路（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 14. The Owl'

summary.en: A woman told to fetch water too often fastens her husband's eagle-feathers along her arms and flies away; the father, learning the cause, reprimands his children and leaves them — he was a Bow. Alone, the girl carries her small brother toward an old canoe-maker across the river, but night brings the Screech-Owl, who kills everybody on the trail and is particularly on the lookout for children. Turning into worms under the grass fails; the Owl picks them into her basket, until the children make themselves heavy and the girl shouts, 'A widow's children are burning up!' — the Owl hangs up the basket and runs home to her five children, and the girl kicks the basket to pieces and makes for the river. The old man stretches his foot across the water and ferries them over; when the Owl comes, he has the Crawfish, the Mussel and the Butterfly ferry her in a thin canoe, telling her to tie many rocks to herself — at midstream the Crawfish splits the canoe, and they hold her under water until she is drowned.
summary.zh: 婦人嫌兒女不為取水，怒繫夫之鷹羽於臂，化鴞飛去。父歸知其故，斥兒女而離——彼本為弓。孤女背弟往投河彼岸老造舟師，夜遇號鴞——此鴞專殺路人，尤嗜孩童。化蟲伏草仍被識破，收入提籃；兄妹自重其身，女呼『寡婦之子焚矣！』鴞掛籃奔家視其五子；女踢碎籃，負弟奔河。老師以足為橋渡之。鴞追至，老師命蝦、蚌、蝶以薄舟渡之，誘其繫石自重；至中流，蝦折其舟，鴞落水，被按於水底，直至溺斃。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Once upon a time there were a man and a woman who had two children, a boy and a girl. The girl was quite tall, but the boy was still quite small. The man used to go on long hunts, and the woman used to dig roots; whenever they went to work, they left the children at home alone. One day the woman came home quite late; she was very thirsty, and asked the children to get her some water. In spite of her repeated orders, they refused to go. Finally she became very angry, and said she would fly away: she fastened along her arms her husband's eagle-feathers, which were hanging on the wall, and flew off. The children cried, begging her to come back, and promised to obey her; but it was too late. She refused to return. The children wept bitterly; when the man came home and asked for their mother, they told him that she had taken his eagle-feathers and flown away. The father, on learning the cause, reprimanded his children and left them. He was a Bow.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 176 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The children were now all alone, and cried all night long. They had an old relative, a maker of canoes, who lived a few miles away, across the river; the girl suggested that they should go to the old man and stay there. She put the boy on her back and started off. Night fell, and the Screech-Owl — who kills everybody that comes along, and who is particularly on the lookout for children — met them on the trail. When the girl saw her, she jumped to one side, but not before the Screech-Owl had seen them. 'Let us turn into worms and crawl under the grass!' They did so; the Owl, however, looked for them, found their tracks, separated the grass, and saw the worms. She concluded that these must be the children, and put them into the basket she had brought for the purpose, and started for home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 176 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: She had gone but a short distance when the children made themselves very heavy. The girl shouted, 'A widow's children are burning up! A widow's children are burning up!' The Owl heard this, and thought, 'Those are surely my five children.' She hung up the basket and ran on home. Just as soon as she was out of sight, the children tried to get down; the girl kicked the basket to pieces, put the boy on her back, and made for the river. When she arrived there, she saw an old man on the opposite bank making a canoe; she called to him to come and take them across, and told him that the Owl was coming. 'Are you my only grand-children?' — 'We are the ones,' the girl replied. Then he stretched his foot across the river; the children stepped on it and held on very firmly, while he doubled it up and so transferred them to the other side.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 176-177 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Owl, in the meantime, had reached her home, and had found her children in no danger whatsoever. She went back to get the boy and the girl; but when she arrived, she found her basket broken and the children gone, and followed their tracks. The old man saw her coming, having recognized her at a distance by her long hair. She asked him if he had seen two children pass that way; the old man merely kept on hammering. 'Why don't you listen?' asked the Owl. The old man told her that he had eaten the children. Then she asked him to ferry her across in a canoe. The old man now decided to kill her: he told the Crawfish, the Mussel, and the Butterfly to ferry the Owl across in a thin canoe; when they reached her, they were to tell her to tie many rocks to herself in order to weight the boat properly, and when they arrived at the centre of the river, the Crawfish was to split the canoe in two. The three set out; they told her to tie rocks to her body, and she did as she was told, and they embarked. When they reached the middle of the river, the Crawfish, in accordance with his instructions, broke the canoe. The Owl fell into the water; she held up a stick that she had carried with her. They seized it and kept her under water until she was drowned. That is the end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 177 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: How Rabbit Got His Wife: The Boy who Split the Thunder-Cloud

region.en: Camas prairie near Mount Idaho, Thunder's camp (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛達荷山附近卡瑪斯草原，雷神之營（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 15. How Rabbit got his Wife'

summary.en: Rabbit's grandson goes up to the camas prairie near Mount Idaho where Thunder keeps five wives taken from other men, carrying the claws of a grizzly bear. Asked which wife Thunder likes best, the diggers point to the oldest, in the colored dress; the boy tells her to throw away her digging-stick and sack, and at the laughing suggestion of the others she does — and he seizes her arms and drags her off while the others fail to rescue her. Thunder hears, paints himself, goes up into the clouds thundering all the time; the storm rages over the fleeing boy, lightning striking everywhere, until the boy looks up and says, 'That is enough for you,' strikes the cloud with his grizzly-bear foot — it splits apart, and Thunder falls to the ground. 'You can take the woman, for I know I cannot get her back'; and the boy went home with his wife.
summary.zh: 兔之孫携灰熊爪上卡瑪斯草原，至雷神之營——其五妻皆奪自他人。掘根之婦告之：雷神最寵穿彩衣之長妻。少年命其棄掘杖與囊；眾婦戲曰：『丟了玩玩，看這小子怎樣！』婦從之，少年即執其臂而擄之，眾婦救之不得。雷神聞訊，繪面登雲，雷聲不絕；狂風暴雨隨少年而行，閃電四擊。少年仰望曰：『足矣！』以灰熊爪擊雲，雲裂，雷神墜地。雷神曰：『女子歸你，吾知不能奪回。』少年遂携妻而歸。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Rabbit lived with his grandson on John Creek, near Snake River. On a camas prairie, near Mount Idaho, lived Thunder, who had five wives that he had taken from other men. The boy decided to go and see him; he took the claws of a grizzly bear with him, and then went up. When he arrived near Thunder's tent, he saw a number of women digging roots. He asked them which of his five wives Thunder liked best, and they told him that he was fondest of the oldest one, with the colored dress. Thereupon the boy went up to her and asked her not to dig any more roots, but to throw away her digging-stick and her sack. The woman laughed, and told the others that the boy was making fun of her. 'Throw it away for fun,' the others said, 'and see what he will do.' So she threw them down, and the boy seized her arms and dragged her off. The others tried to rescue her, but were unsuccessful; then they sent word to Thunder, telling him that one of his wives had been stolen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 177-178 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Thunder heard this, he made ready to pursue Rabbit. He painted himself, and a thunder-clap was heard; then he went up into the clouds, thundering all the time. The boy was hastening away; the thunder-cloud stood right over him, and a terrific storm raged, the lightning striking everywhere. The abducted woman cried, for she was afraid that she would be killed; the boy, however, paid no attention to it all. After a time the boy looked up, and said to Thunder, 'That is enough for you.' He took his grizzly-bear foot and struck the cloud with it; the cloud split apart, and Thunder fell down to the ground. 'You can take the woman,' he then said to the boy, 'for I know I cannot get her back.' So the boy went home with his wife. When he arrived there, he left her outside, while he went in and told his grandmother that he had brought a wife; the old woman brought the young one in, and they lived there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 178 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Origin of Death: Coyote Follows His Daughter's Voice
title.zh: 死亡之始：郊狼隨女聲而行

region.en: Trail to the land of the dead by the sea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 通往海濱亡者之國的路（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 16. The Origin of Death'

summary.en: Coyote's married daughter is accidentally burned to death, and her husband moves away leaving him alone; one night his daughter comes and talks to him: 'I have just come to see you. I am going on to where the dead people live. You cannot go with us, because you are alive, and we are dead.' Told he may come if he throws himself into the fire, Coyote jumps into the flames, jumps out at the pain, and is so badly blistered that his daughter allows him along: 'You will never see us again, but you will hear us later. There is nothing to eat on the trail. You must stick your hand in your mouth. That will satisfy you.' For ten days he follows her voice — into rocks and trees, laughing ahead of him, invisible in daylight. At the land of the dead, close to the sea, they fear they must bar him because he is alive, and make him sleep apart; the bag of eggs he gathers falls through its own holes until his daughter teaches him to tie it up — and henceforth it became his duty to gather eggs.
summary.zh: 郊狼之女誤遭火焚而死，其夫遷走，郊狼獨居。一夜亡女來訪：『吾來看你。吾將往亡者之鄉。爾係生人，不得同行。』又言：『若投火自焚，可隨吾行。』郊狼躍入火中，痛極而出，灼傷甚重，女乃允其同行：『爾從此不得見吾等，唯能聞其聲。途中無食，可自吮己手以充飢。』十日之間，郊狼循聲而行——穿巖繞樹，笑聲在前，白晝一無所見。至亡者之國，近海之地，亡者懼其生，令之別宿。彼拾蛋盈袋，然袋皆孔，蛋盡漏；女教之繫緊囊口，果然蛋至家中滿滿一袋——郊狼從此以拾蛋為業。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Journey to the land of the dead. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote's married daughter was accidentally burned to death. Her husband moved away, and left Coyote alone. One night, as Coyote was sleeping, his daughter came and talked to him: 'I have just come to see you. I am going on to where the dead people live. You cannot go with us, because you are alive, and we are dead.' Coyote said that he would follow her. 'You can come along if you throw yourself into the fire,' the girl told him. Coyote threw himself into the flames; but as soon as he felt the pain, he jumped out again. He was so badly blistered, however, that his daughter allowed him to go along. 'You will never see us again,' she told him, 'but you will hear us later. There is nothing to eat on the trail. You must stick your hand in your mouth. That will satisfy you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 178 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The girl led the way, and Coyote followed her voice. It often led him into rocks and trees. There was the noise of laughter ahead of him, and Coyote followed the sound. Though it was daylight, Coyote could see nothing; they talked only when evening came, and then Coyote would follow the sound. They travelled for five days; at the end of that time Coyote could almost see them, and in five days more they would be like people to him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 178 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: When they finally arrived at the land of the dead, they feared they would have to bar him from it, because he was alive; they made him sleep at some distance from the others. The land of the dead was very close to the sea. All about him Coyote saw all kinds of eggs; they gave him a bag full of holes in which to gather eggs. He filled the bag, and saw that all the eggs fell through the holes; therefore he did not even tie it up. When he came back to his daughter, he had nothing at all. The girl then said to him, 'Next time fill up the bag; and even if it falls together, as if there were nothing in it, be sure to tie it up. Then it will be full.' — 'That is what I thought,' replied Coyote. He went back to gather more eggs; he filled the bag and tied it up. He threw it on his back, but it seemed as though there were nothing in it; soon, however, it grew heavy, and when he reached the house, it was quite full. Henceforth it became his duty to gather eggs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 178-179 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
